q: Which sequence lists ecological levels of organization from the smallest to the largest?
o: Organism, population, community, ecosystem
Organism, population, ecosystem, community
Organism, community, population, ecosystem
Population, organism, community, ecosystem
w: One organism belongs to a population (one species), populations form a community (many species), and a community plus its nonliving environment is an ecosystem.

n.1: Community and ecosystem are swapped: an ecosystem is a community plus the nonliving environment.
n.2: Population and community are swapped: one species comes before all species together.
n.3: A population is made of many organisms, so the organism comes first.

q: A bean seed has sat unchanged in a jar for two years. Which observation would best show that the seed is alive?
o: Its cells use energy and divide after watering.
It has a hard, protective outer coat.
It gains mass after soaking in water overnight.
It is built from carbon-containing molecules.
w: Living things are made of cells that use energy (metabolism) and grow by cell division. A seed whose cells start respiring and dividing after watering is alive.

n.1: A hard coat protects the embryo, but nonliving objects such as shells and stones also have hard coverings.
n.2: Gaining mass by soaking up water is absorption; a dry sponge does the same without being alive.
n.3: Dead wood, paper and oil are also built from carbon compounds, so this does not show life.

q: Why are viruses not classified in any of the three domains of life (Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya)?
o: They do not change over generations.
They are not made of cells.
They contain no genetic material.
They are prokaryotes, like bacteria.
w: The domains classify cellular life. Viruses are not made of cells: they are genetic material in a protein coat and reproduce inside host cells.

n.0: Viruses do change over generations; their genes mutate and the populations evolve.
n.2: Viruses do carry genetic material (DNA or RNA); that is how they direct host cells to make new viruses.
n.3: Prokaryotes are cells without a nucleus; viruses are not cells at all.

q: Mushrooms were once grouped with plants. Which feature shows that fungi belong in a separate kingdom?
o: They absorb food and have walls of chitin.
They lack a nucleus and membrane organelles.
They make food and have walls of cellulose.
They ingest food and have no cell walls.
w: Fungi are heterotrophs that absorb food from their surroundings, and their cell walls are made of chitin. Plants make their own food and have cellulose walls.

n.1: Fungi are eukaryotes with a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles; lacking them describes prokaryotes.
n.2: Making food by photosynthesis and having cellulose walls describes plants, not fungi.
n.3: Ingesting food with no cell walls describes animals; fungi have chitin walls and absorb food.

q: Which pair of organisms are both autotrophs?
o: A fern and a bread yeast
A grass and an amoeba
A moss and a green alga
A pine tree and a mushroom
w: Autotrophs make their own food, usually by photosynthesis. Mosses and green algae both contain chlorophyll and photosynthesize.

n.0: The fern is an autotroph, but yeast is a fungus, a heterotroph.
n.1: Grass is an autotroph, but an amoeba is a protist that engulfs food, a heterotroph.
n.3: The pine is an autotroph, but a mushroom is a fungus, a heterotroph that absorbs food.

q: After years of heavy antibiotic use, most bacteria of one species in a hospital are resistant. Which explanation fits natural selection?
o: The antibiotic caused new resistance mutations in the cells.
Each bacterium developed resistance because it needed it.
Resistant bacteria already present survived and multiplied.
Bacteria exposed to the drug grew tougher and passed it on.
w: Resistance alleles already existed in a few bacteria. The antibiotic killed the susceptible cells, the resistant ones survived and reproduced, and over generations the population became mostly resistant.

n.0: The antibiotic does not cause the mutation; it selects bacteria that already carried resistance.
n.1: Organisms do not develop traits because they need them; the variation must exist first.
n.3: Toughening during an organism's life is an acquired trait, and acquired traits are not inherited.

q: In a population of white-tailed deer, which individual has the highest evolutionary fitness?
o: The oldest doe, which raised one fawn
The fastest buck, which outran every predator
The largest buck, which wins the most fights
A doe that raised five fawns that later bred
w: Fitness is reproductive success: the number of surviving, fertile offspring an individual leaves. The doe with five breeding fawns passes on the most alleles.

n.0: A long life with one fawn passes on fewer alleles than five fawns that breed.
n.1: Escaping predators helps survival, but fitness is measured in offspring, not speed.
n.2: Size and strength are not fitness unless they produce more surviving offspring.

q: A bird wing and a butterfly wing both allow flight, but they develop from very different structures. Which description fits them?
o: Homologous: they evolved separately for one use
Homologous: they show a recent common ancestor
Analogous: they evolved separately for one use
Vestigial: they are reduced and no longer used
w: Analogous structures share a function but differ in origin, so they evolved independently. Homologous structures share an underlying structure from a common ancestor.

n.0: Evolving separately for a similar use defines analogous, not homologous, structures.
n.1: Homologous structures share the same underlying anatomy, which bird and insect wings do not.
n.3: Vestigial structures are reduced remnants; both wings are fully working.

q: A weightlifter builds large muscles over ten years of training. According to modern evolutionary theory, how will this affect his future children?
o: Their muscles will be larger from birth.
They will inherit part of his extra muscle.
It will have no effect on the traits they inherit.
They will build muscle faster when they train.
w: Traits acquired during life, such as trained muscles, do not change the DNA in sperm, so they are not inherited (Lamarck's idea was rejected).

n.0: Larger muscles at birth would require inherited acquired traits, which do not occur.
n.1: Muscle gained by training changes body tissue, not the genes in sperm, so none of it is inherited.
n.3: His training does not alter the alleles he passes on, so it does not speed his children's muscle growth.

q: Which statement about evolution by natural selection is accurate?
o: Individual organisms evolve during their lifetimes.
Populations evolve as heritable traits change in frequency.
Natural selection creates the variation that it acts on.
Traits change because organisms try to adapt to change.
w: Evolution is a change in the inherited traits (allele frequencies) of a population over generations. Selection acts on variation that already exists.

n.0: Individuals do not evolve; populations change over generations.
n.2: Variation comes from mutation and sexual reproduction; selection only sorts it.
n.3: Organisms do not change their inherited traits by trying; adaptation results from selection of existing variation.

q: A storm randomly kills most of the lizards on a small island, and the few survivors carry rare alleles by chance. Which mechanism changes allele frequencies here?
o: Gene flow
Natural selection
Genetic drift
Artificial selection
w: Random events that change allele frequencies are genetic drift; a sudden random loss of most of a population is the bottleneck effect, strongest in small populations.

n.0: Gene flow is the movement of alleles between populations by migration.
n.1: Natural selection is nonrandom: survivors would have traits that helped them survive the storm.
n.3: Artificial selection is humans choosing which organisms breed.

q: Very small and large eggs of one bird species hatch less often than medium eggs, so over generations egg size clusters near the middle. Which type of selection is this?
o: Stabilizing selection
Directional selection
Disruptive selection
Artificial selection
w: Stabilizing selection favors the average and acts against both extremes, so the range narrows around the middle.

n.1: Directional selection favors one extreme, shifting the average one way.
n.2: Disruptive selection favors both extremes over the average, the reverse of this case.
n.3: Artificial selection is breeding chosen by humans; here survival in nature decides.

q: Human DNA sequences match chimpanzee DNA far more closely than mouse DNA. Which line of evidence for evolution does this comparison provide?
o: The fossil record
Comparative embryology
Molecular biology
Biogeography
w: Similarity in DNA and protein sequences is molecular evidence: more closely related species share more of their sequences.

n.0: The fossil record is preserved remains in rock layers, not DNA comparisons.
n.1: Comparative embryology compares early embryos, not DNA sequences.
n.3: Biogeography is the distribution of species across places on Earth.

q: Two populations of one squirrel species are separated by a canyon for thousands of generations. Later they can no longer interbreed. What has most likely occurred?
o: Artificial selection, so humans bred them apart
Speciation, so they are now separate species
Stabilizing selection, so they stayed one species
Gene flow, so the gene pools merged into one
w: Geographic isolation stopped gene flow, the populations diverged, and they became reproductively isolated: new species formed (speciation).

n.0: Artificial selection requires humans choosing breeders, which the stem does not describe.
n.2: Stabilizing selection favors average traits within a population; these groups diverged and can no longer interbreed.
n.3: The canyon blocked gene flow; merged gene pools would leave the groups able to interbreed.

q: In a water molecule, which atom carries a partial negative charge, and why?
o: Hydrogen, since it attracts shared electrons more
Oxygen, since it gives its electrons to hydrogen
Neither, since water is a nonpolar molecule
Oxygen, since it attracts shared electrons more
w: Oxygen is more electronegative than hydrogen, so the shared electrons spend more time near it. Oxygen becomes partially negative and each hydrogen partially positive: water is polar.

n.0: Hydrogen attracts electrons less strongly, so it carries the partial positive charge.
n.1: Electrons are shared unequally in polar covalent bonds, not transferred as in an ionic bond.
n.2: Water is polar; its bent shape and unequal sharing give it partial charges.

q: Which bonds hold neighboring molecules together in liquid water?
o: Polar covalent bonds sharing electrons
Ionic bonds between H+ and OH- ions
Hydrogen bonds between partial charges
Nonpolar covalent bonds between oxygens
w: Hydrogen bonds form between the partially positive hydrogen of one molecule and the partially negative oxygen of a neighbor. They are weak one by one but strong together.

n.0: Polar covalent bonds join oxygen and hydrogen inside each molecule, not neighboring molecules.
n.1: Water ionizes only slightly; liquid water is held together by hydrogen bonds, not ionic bonds.
n.3: Oxygen atoms of neighboring molecules do not share electrons; the attraction is hydrogen bonding.

q: A water strider walks across the surface of a pond without sinking. Which property of water makes this possible?
o: Adhesion, which pulls water up its legs
Capillary action along the water surface
Cohesion, which creates surface tension
High specific heat of the surface layer
w: Hydrogen bonds make water molecules stick to each other (cohesion), producing surface tension strong enough to support a light insect.

n.0: Adhesion is water sticking to other surfaces; it would wet the legs rather than hold the insect up.
n.1: Capillary action is water rising in narrow tubes, not support on an open surface.
n.3: Specific heat concerns resistance to temperature change, not support of weight.

q: Water climbs the inside of a narrow glass tube because its molecules are attracted to the glass. What is this attraction called?
o: Specific heat
Cohesion
Surface tension
Adhesion
w: Adhesion is the attraction of water to other polar surfaces such as glass; together with cohesion it produces capillary action.

n.0: Specific heat is the heat needed to change water's temperature.
n.1: Cohesion is water attracted to water, not to the glass.
n.2: Surface tension is a result of cohesion at the water's surface.

q: Towns beside a large lake have milder temperature swings than towns farther inland. Which property of water best explains this?
o: Its low density as ice
Its high specific heat
Its strong cohesion
Its low specific heat
w: Water's high specific heat lets it absorb and release large amounts of heat with little change in its own temperature, which moderates the nearby climate.

n.0: Floating ice insulates the water below but does not explain milder air temperatures year-round.
n.2: Cohesion produces surface tension; it does not store heat.
n.3: Low specific heat would make the lake heat and cool quickly, worsening the swings.

q: Sweating cools a runner during a long race. Which property of water most directly explains the cooling?
o: High heat of vaporization
High specific heat
Strong adhesion to skin
Low freezing point
w: Evaporating water absorbs a large amount of heat (high heat of vaporization), carrying heat away from the skin: evaporative cooling.

n.1: Specific heat is resistance to temperature change; the cooling here comes from evaporation.
n.2: Adhesion keeps sweat on the skin but does not remove heat.
n.3: Water's freezing point does not affect cooling of the skin on a warm day.

q: A pond freezes at the surface while fish survive in the water below. Why does ice float on liquid water?
o: Ice traps more dissolved air, which makes it lighter.
Freezing breaks hydrogen bonds and spreads molecules out.
Hydrogen bonds hold ice in an open, less dense lattice.
Ice is denser but held up by surface tension.
w: As water freezes, each molecule hydrogen-bonds to its neighbors in a rigid, open lattice. The molecules are farther apart than in the liquid, so ice is less dense and floats.

n.0: Low density comes from the hydrogen-bonded lattice, not from trapped air.
n.1: Freezing forms stable hydrogen bonds; it does not break them.
n.3: Ice is less dense than liquid water; surface tension could not hold up a sheet of ice.

q: Salad oil forms a separate layer on a water-based dressing. Which statement explains why the oil does not dissolve in the water?
o: Oil is polar, so its charges repel the charges of water.
Oil is ionic, so its ions bond too tightly to separate.
Oil is less dense, so it floats and cannot mix with water.
Oil is nonpolar, so it cannot hydrogen bond with water.
w: Water dissolves polar and ionic substances (hydrophilic). Oils are nonpolar (hydrophobic) and cannot form hydrogen bonds with water, so they separate.

n.0: Polar substances dissolve in water; oils fail to dissolve because they are nonpolar.
n.1: Oils are not ionic, and ionic compounds such as salt dissolve readily in water.
n.2: Density explains why the layer sits on top, not why the oil fails to dissolve.

q: Pure water has a pH of 7. Which statement explains this neutral pH?
o: Its polar charges cancel out any H+ ions.
It ionizes into more OH- than H+ ions.
It does not ionize, so no ions are present.
It ionizes slightly into equal H+ and OH-.
w: A few water molecules split into H+ (as H3O+) and OH-. In pure water the two are equal, so the solution is neutral, pH 7.

n.0: Partial charges on molecules do not remove H+ ions; neutrality comes from equal H+ and OH-.
n.1: More OH- than H+ would make the solution basic, above pH 7.
n.2: Water does ionize slightly; that small amount of H+ and OH- gives pH 7.

q: After a large meal, a person's liver and skeletal muscles store excess glucose as a highly branched polysaccharide. Which molecule is formed?
o: Glycogen
Starch
Cellulose
Chitin
w: Animals store glucose as glycogen in the liver and muscles. Starch is the plant storage form.

n.1: Starch is the storage polysaccharide of plants, not animals.
n.2: Cellulose is a structural polysaccharide in plant cell walls.
n.3: Chitin is a structural polysaccharide in fungal walls and insect exoskeletons.

q: A lab analysis shows that an unknown macromolecule from a cell contains carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen, but no phosphorus. Which type of macromolecule is it most likely to be?
o: A nucleic acid
A protein
A carbohydrate
A phospholipid
w: Step 1: nitrogen rules out carbohydrates and simple fats. Step 2: the absence of phosphorus rules out nucleic acids and phospholipids, leaving protein (C, H, O, N, often S).

n.0: Nucleic acids contain phosphorus in their phosphate groups.
n.2: Common carbohydrates such as sugars, starch and glycogen contain only C, H and O, so nitrogen points away from them.
n.3: Phospholipids contain a phosphate group, so phosphorus would be present.

q: Butter is solid at room temperature, while olive oil is liquid. Which difference in their fatty acids best explains this?
o: Butter's fats contain more glycerol molecules per fatty acid.
Olive oil's fatty acids carry more hydrogen atoms per carbon.
Butter's fatty acids are mostly saturated and pack tightly together.
Butter's fatty acids have more C=C double bonds, which form kinks.
w: Saturated fatty acids have no C=C double bonds, so their straight chains pack tightly and the fat is solid. Unsaturated fatty acids in oils have double bonds that kink the chains.

n.0: Every triglyceride has one glycerol and three fatty acids; the difference is saturation.
n.1: This is reversed: saturated fatty acids such as butter's carry the most hydrogen. Olive oil's C=C double bonds mean fewer hydrogens.
n.3: This is reversed: double bonds and kinks belong to unsaturated fats, which are liquid.

q: Two glucose molecules are joined to form the disaccharide maltose. Which description of this reaction is correct?
o: A water molecule is released, forming a peptide bond.
A water molecule is released, forming a glycosidic bond.
A water molecule is added, forming a peptide bond.
A water molecule is added, forming a glycosidic bond.
w: Monomers are joined by dehydration synthesis, which releases water. Bonds between sugars are glycosidic bonds.

n.0: Peptide bonds join amino acids, not sugars.
n.2: This combines both errors: adding water breaks bonds, and peptide bonds join amino acids.
n.3: Adding water is hydrolysis, which breaks polymers apart rather than joining them.

q: A patient with lactose intolerance makes too little lactase. When lactase does digest lactose, which two monosaccharides are released?
o: Glucose and galactose
Galactose and fructose
Glucose and glucose
Glucose and fructose
w: Lactose (milk sugar) = glucose + galactose. Lactase hydrolyzes it into those two monosaccharides.

n.1: Galactose + fructose is not one of the common dietary disaccharides.
n.2: Glucose + glucose make maltose.
n.3: Glucose + fructose make sucrose (table sugar).

q: When phospholipids are placed in water, they arrange themselves into a double layer. Which feature of phospholipid structure explains this arrangement?
o: Their tails are polar and are attracted to the surrounding water.
Their hydrophilic heads face water while hydrophobic tails face inward.
Their three fatty acid tails make them dissolve in water.
Their nonpolar heads face water while polar tails face inward.
w: A phospholipid has a hydrophilic (polar) phosphate head and two hydrophobic (nonpolar) fatty acid tails. In water the heads face outward and the tails hide inside, forming a bilayer.

n.0: The fatty acid tails are nonpolar and hydrophobic, so they avoid water.
n.2: Phospholipids have two fatty acid tails (triglycerides have three), and the tails repel water.
n.3: Polarity is reversed: the heads are polar and the tails are nonpolar.

q: Hemoglobin is built from four polypeptide chains fitted together into one working molecule. Which level of protein structure describes this arrangement?
o: Tertiary structure
Secondary structure
Primary structure
Quaternary structure
w: Quaternary structure is the arrangement of two or more polypeptide chains in one protein, as in hemoglobin's four chains.

n.0: Tertiary structure is the 3-D folding of a single chain.
n.1: Secondary structure is local coiling and folding (alpha helix, beta sheet) held by hydrogen bonds.
n.2: Primary structure is the amino acid sequence of one chain.

q: When an egg white is cooked, the protein albumin turns from clear to opaque white and does not return to its original form on cooling. What happened?
o: Its amino acid sequence was rearranged.
It was denatured and lost its folded shape.
It gained new amino acids from the heat.
Its peptide bonds broke into free amino acids.
w: Heat denatures proteins: it disrupts the bonds that hold the folded shape, so the protein unfolds and loses its function. The peptide bonds and sequence stay intact.

n.0: The primary sequence is unchanged by denaturation; only the folding is lost.
n.2: Heating adds no amino acids; the same chain unfolds.
n.3: Denaturation leaves peptide bonds intact; breaking them would require hydrolysis.

q: Cholesterol, testosterone and cortisol share a structure of four fused carbon rings. To which class of biological molecule do they belong?
o: Lipids
Proteins
Carbohydrates
Nucleic acids
w: Steroids, built on four fused rings, are lipids. Cholesterol is the starting point for steroid hormones such as testosterone and cortisol.

n.1: Some hormones, such as insulin, are proteins, but steroid hormones are lipids.
n.2: Carbohydrates are sugars and their polymers, not fused-ring steroids.
n.3: Nucleic acids are chains of nucleotides that store genetic information.

q: Which pairing of polymer, monomer and bond is correct?
o: Glycogen, amino acids, glycosidic bonds
DNA, nucleotides, phosphodiester bonds
Starch, glucose, peptide bonds
Protein, amino acids, glycosidic bonds
w: DNA is a polymer of nucleotides linked by phosphodiester bonds. Proteins use peptide bonds between amino acids; polysaccharides use glycosidic bonds between sugars.

n.0: Glycogen is built from glucose, not amino acids.
n.2: Glucose units in starch are joined by glycosidic bonds; peptide bonds join amino acids.
n.3: Amino acids in proteins are joined by peptide bonds, not glycosidic bonds.

q: In the first minutes of intense exercise, which class of macromolecule do muscle cells use as their main quick source of energy?
o: Nucleic acids, such as RNA
Lipids, such as triglycerides
Carbohydrates, such as glucose
Proteins, such as myosin
w: Carbohydrates (glucose and stored glycogen) are the main quick energy source. Lipids store the most energy per gram but are long-term fuel.

n.0: Nucleic acids carry genetic information, not fuel.
n.1: Triglycerides hold more energy per gram but are long-term storage, released more slowly.
n.3: Myosin is a contractile protein; proteins are not the preferred fuel.

q: Human proteins are built from 20 different amino acids. Which part of an amino acid differs from one kind to the next?
o: The carboxyl group
The amino group
The R group
The central carbon atom
w: Every amino acid has a central carbon with an amino group, a carboxyl group and a hydrogen; the variable R group (side chain) gives each kind its properties.

n.0: All amino acids share the same carboxyl group.
n.1: All amino acids share the same amino group.
n.3: Every amino acid has the same central (alpha) carbon; the R group attached to it is what varies.

q: Energy for a muscle contraction is released when a cell converts ATP into ADP and an inorganic phosphate. Which bond is broken in this reaction?
o: The bond between the first and second phosphates
The bond between ribose and the first phosphate
The bond holding the last phosphate group
The bond between adenine and ribose
w: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) releases usable energy when the bond to its last (third) phosphate is hydrolyzed, giving ADP + Pi.

n.0: Breaking between the first and second phosphates would release two phosphates together and leave AMP, not ADP + Pi.
n.1: Losing the first phosphate would remove all three phosphates at once, not form ADP.
n.3: Breaking the adenine-ribose bond would destroy the nucleoside rather than form ADP.

q: The rate of a human enzyme-catalyzed reaction rises as the temperature increases from 20 °C to 37 °C, then drops sharply at 50 °C. What best explains the drop?
o: The heat raises the activation energy of the reaction.
The enzyme denatures, and its active site loses its shape.
The enzyme is used up as it converts more of the substrate.
The heat breaks the peptide bonds in the enzyme's chain.
w: Above its optimum (about 37 °C for most human enzymes) the enzyme denatures: its folding is disrupted, the active site changes shape, and the substrate no longer fits.

n.0: Enzymes work by lowering activation energy. The drop is due to loss of enzyme shape, not a change in activation energy.
n.2: Enzymes are catalysts and are not consumed by the reactions they speed up.
n.3: Denaturation disrupts folding; the peptide bonds of the primary sequence stay intact.

q: In liver cells, the enzyme catalase greatly speeds up the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen. How does catalase increase the reaction rate?
o: It increases the total energy the reaction releases.
It is consumed and becomes part of the products.
It shifts the equilibrium toward more products.
It lowers the activation energy of the reaction.
w: Enzymes are biological catalysts: they lower activation energy, are not consumed, and do not change the overall energy released.

n.0: Enzymes do not change the overall energy change of the reaction, only the energy needed to start it.
n.1: Enzymes are not consumed; they are released unchanged and reused.
n.2: Enzymes do not change the equilibrium of a reaction; they help it reach equilibrium faster.

q: Pepsin works in the stomach at about pH 2. If pepsin passes into the small intestine, where the pH is about 8, what will most likely happen to its activity?
o: It will rise, since trypsin activates pepsin at pH 8.
It will stay the same, since a catalyst is not used up.
It will fall, since pH 8 is far from pepsin's optimum.
It will rise, since enzymes work faster in basic solutions.
w: Each enzyme has an optimum pH. Pepsin works best near pH 2, so at pH 8 its shape changes and activity falls. Trypsin, with an optimum near pH 8, works in the small intestine.

n.0: Trypsin is a separate protein-digesting enzyme with its own optimum; it does not boost pepsin.
n.1: Catalysts are not consumed, but that does not protect pepsin's shape: at pH 8, far from its optimum, the enzyme loses activity.
n.3: Enzymes do not all work faster in basic conditions; each has its own optimum, and pepsin's is acidic.

q: A drug shaped like an enzyme's substrate binds the active site and slows the reaction. Adding much more substrate restores the normal rate. Which type of inhibition is this?
o: Noncompetitive inhibition
Competitive inhibition
Denaturation by heat
Substrate saturation
w: A competitive inhibitor binds the active site and competes with the substrate, so raising substrate concentration can overcome it.

n.0: A noncompetitive (allosteric) inhibitor binds elsewhere and changes the enzyme's shape; extra substrate does not overcome it.
n.2: Denaturation is loss of enzyme shape from heat or extreme pH, not binding of an inhibitor.
n.3: Saturation is the plateau reached when all active sites are busy; it is not inhibition.

q: After a meal, liver cells link many glucose molecules into glycogen. How is this process classified?
o: Anabolic: it builds a polymer and uses energy
Anabolic: it builds a polymer and releases energy
Catabolic: it builds a polymer and uses energy
Catabolic: it breaks bonds and releases energy
w: Anabolism builds larger molecules from smaller ones and requires energy. Making glycogen from glucose is anabolic.

n.1: Building a polymer requires energy; releasing energy is a feature of catabolism.
n.2: Catabolism breaks molecules down; building glycogen is anabolism.
n.3: Glycogen synthesis builds, not breaks, bonds between glucose units.

q: A heavy-metal ion binds to an enzyme away from its active site and changes the enzyme's shape. Adding more substrate does not restore activity. What is this?
o: Feedback (end-product) inhibition
Substrate saturation
Competitive inhibition
Noncompetitive inhibition
w: A noncompetitive (allosteric) inhibitor binds elsewhere on the enzyme and changes its shape, so extra substrate cannot overcome it.

n.0: Feedback inhibition is a pathway's end product slowing an early enzyme, not a heavy-metal ion.
n.1: Saturation is the plateau when all active sites are full; it is not inhibition.
n.2: A competitive inhibitor binds the active site, and more substrate can outcompete it.

q: In a five-step metabolic pathway, the final product binds to the first enzyme and slows it when the product builds up. What is this control called?
o: Feedback inhibition
Positive feedback
Substrate saturation
Enzyme denaturation
w: In feedback inhibition, the end product of a pathway inhibits an early enzyme, so the cell stops making more product than it needs.

n.1: Positive feedback would speed the pathway as product builds up, the reverse of this.
n.2: Saturation is all active sites filled by substrate, not inhibition by a product.
n.3: Denaturation is loss of shape from heat or extreme pH, not regulation by a product.

q: As substrate concentration rises, an enzyme's reaction rate increases and then levels off. Which explanation best accounts for the plateau?
o: All of the active sites are occupied.
The extra substrate denatures the enzyme.
The activation energy rises too high.
The enzyme is used up by the reaction.
w: Once every active site is busy (saturation), adding substrate cannot raise the rate further; only more enzyme could.

n.1: Substrate does not denature enzymes; heat and extreme pH do.
n.2: Activation energy does not change with substrate concentration; the enzyme keeps lowering it.
n.3: Enzymes are not consumed; they are released unchanged and reused.

q: Lactase breaks down lactose but has no effect on sucrose. What best explains this specificity?
o: Sucrose denatures lactase's active site.
Lactase is used up by lactose before sucrose.
Sucrose does not fit lactase's active site.
Sucrose raises lactase's activation energy.
w: An enzyme's active site matches the shape of its own substrate (lock-and-key, induced fit). Sucrose does not fit lactase's active site, so it is not broken down.

n.0: Sucrose does not unfold the enzyme; it simply does not bind.
n.1: Enzymes are not consumed by the reactions they catalyze.
n.3: Enzymes lower activation energy; a substrate does not raise it.

q: How do ATP and ADP differ in structure?
o: ATP contains adenine; ADP contains guanine.
ATP has three phosphate groups; ADP has two.
ATP has two phosphate groups; ADP has three.
ATP contains ribose; ADP contains deoxyribose.
w: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) has three phosphate groups. Removing one by hydrolysis gives ADP (adenosine diphosphate) + Pi and releases energy.

n.0: Both contain adenine; the A in ATP and ADP stands for adenosine.
n.2: The counts are reversed: tri- means three (ATP), di- means two (ADP).
n.3: Both contain ribose; deoxyribose is the sugar in DNA.

q: Which statement about energy conversions in cells agrees with the laws of thermodynamics?
o: Cell energy conversions lose no energy as heat.
Energy in ATP is destroyed when the ATP is used.
Cells create new energy when they break down glucose.
Each conversion releases some energy as heat.
w: Energy is neither created nor destroyed, only converted, and every conversion loses some energy as heat (entropy increases).

n.0: No conversion is perfectly efficient; some energy always escapes as heat.
n.1: Energy cannot be destroyed; ATP's energy is transferred to cell work and heat.
n.2: Energy cannot be created; cells convert chemical energy already stored in glucose.

q: Under an electron microscope, a cell shows a plasma membrane, a cell wall, ribosomes and DNA in a nucleoid region, but no membrane-bound organelles. Which organism is the likely source?
o: A leaf cell from a pea plant
A yeast cell used to leaven bread
A bacterium such as Escherichia coli
A protozoan such as Giardia
w: A nucleoid region in place of a nucleus and the absence of membrane-bound organelles mark a prokaryotic cell. Bacteria are prokaryotes, and most have a cell wall made of peptidoglycan.

n.0: A pea leaf cell has a cell wall, but as a eukaryote it has a nucleus, chloroplasts and mitochondria.
n.1: Yeast is a fungus, a eukaryote. It has a cell wall (chitin) but also a membrane-bound nucleus and organelles.
n.3: Giardia is a protozoan, a single-celled eukaryote with a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.

q: A biology student is listing features that prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells have in common. Which feature belongs on the list?
o: Ribosomes that carry out protein synthesis
A nuclear envelope surrounding the DNA
Mitochondria that produce most of the ATP
Linear chromosomes wound around histones
w: Both cell types have a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, DNA and ribosomes. Prokaryotic ribosomes are smaller than eukaryotic ones, but both make proteins.

n.1: A nuclear envelope belongs to eukaryotes. Prokaryotic DNA sits in a nucleoid region with no surrounding membrane.
n.2: Mitochondria are membrane-bound organelles, which prokaryotes lack.
n.3: Linear chromosomes packaged with histones are a eukaryotic feature. Prokaryotes usually have a single circular chromosome.

q: A cut on a patient's arm heals as nearby skin cells divide to replace the damaged ones. Which tenet of cell theory does this observation most directly support?
o: The cell is the basic unit of structure and function in living things.
Cells of the same type group together to form tissues.
All living things are made of one or more cells.
All cells arise from pre-existing cells.
w: New skin cells come from the division of existing skin cells, which is the third tenet of cell theory: all cells come from pre-existing cells.

n.0: This is a real tenet of cell theory, but the observation is about where new cells come from, not about the cell as the unit of function.
n.1: Grouping of cells into tissues describes levels of organization, not one of the three tenets of cell theory.
n.2: This tenet is about what organisms are made of. The healing wound shows the origin of new cells.

q: A slide shows cells with a rigid outer boundary, a large central vacuole and green, disk-shaped organelles. Which other structure would these cells also be expected to contain?
o: A nucleoid region instead of a nucleus
A cell wall made of peptidoglycan
Glycogen granules that store glucose
Mitochondria for cellular respiration
w: The wall, central vacuole and chloroplasts identify a plant cell. Plant cells carry out cellular respiration in mitochondria as well as photosynthesis in chloroplasts.

n.0: A nucleoid region is a prokaryotic feature. Plant cells are eukaryotic and have a membrane-bound nucleus.
n.1: Peptidoglycan walls belong to bacteria. A plant cell wall is made of cellulose.
n.2: Glycogen is the animal storage polysaccharide; plant cells store glucose as starch.

q: A biology tutor writes four statements on the board comparing prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells. Which of the statements is accurate?
o: Prokaryotes divide by mitosis and eukaryotes by binary fission.
Prokaryotic DNA is linear and eukaryotic DNA is one circular loop.
Bacteria have peptidoglycan walls and plants have cellulose walls.
Prokaryotic cells are usually larger than eukaryotic cells.
w: Bacteria (prokaryotes) build their cell walls from peptidoglycan, and plants (eukaryotes) build theirs from cellulose. Each of the other statements reverses a real difference: cell size, method of division and form of the DNA.

n.0: This reverses the methods: prokaryotes divide by binary fission and eukaryotes use mitosis or meiosis.
n.1: This reverses the DNA forms: prokaryotes usually have one circular chromosome and eukaryotes have several linear chromosomes.
n.3: This reverses the sizes: prokaryotic cells are smaller than eukaryotic cells.

q: A lab manual describes cell walls built from cellulose, chitin and peptidoglycan. Which pairing of wall material and cell is correct?
o: Cellulose in the wall of a bacterial cell
Cellulose in the wall of a yeast cell
Peptidoglycan in the wall of a plant cell
Chitin in the wall of a mold cell
w: Molds and yeasts are fungi, and fungal cell walls are made of chitin. Plant walls are cellulose and bacterial walls are peptidoglycan.

n.0: Bacterial walls are made of peptidoglycan, not cellulose.
n.1: Yeast is a fungus, so its wall contains chitin rather than the cellulose found in plants.
n.2: Plant cell walls are made of cellulose. Peptidoglycan is the bacterial wall material.

q: A cell has a membrane-bound nucleus, mitochondria and a cell wall, but no chloroplasts. Of the following, which is the most likely source of this cell?
o: A yeast cell
A Staphylococcus bacterium
A moss leaf cell
A human liver cell
w: Step 1: a nucleus and mitochondria mean the cell is eukaryotic, which rules out bacteria. Step 2: a cell wall without chloroplasts fits a fungus such as yeast, which has a chitin wall and cannot photosynthesize.

n.1: Bacteria have cell walls but are prokaryotes, so they have no nucleus or mitochondria.
n.2: A moss leaf cell has a wall and nucleus, but as a photosynthetic leaf cell it contains chloroplasts.
n.3: Human cells are eukaryotic with mitochondria, but animal cells have no cell wall.

q: A microbe from a hot spring lacks a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, yet genetic testing shows it is not a bacterium. How should it be classified?
o: As a virus, since it lacks organelles
As a eukaryote in the protist group
As a fungus, since it has a cell wall
As a prokaryote in domain Archaea
w: Prokaryotes include two groups, Bacteria and Archaea. A cell with no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles that is not a bacterium is an archaeon.

n.0: Viruses are not cells at all. This microbe is a cell with ribosomes and a membrane, so it is not a virus.
n.1: Protists are eukaryotes, so they have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
n.2: Fungi are eukaryotes with a nucleus, so a cell without a nucleus cannot be a fungus.

q: A researcher compares the DNA of a bacterium with the DNA of a human white blood cell. Which description fits the bacterial DNA?
o: A single circular chromosome, often with plasmids
Several linear chromosomes inside a nuclear envelope
Linear chromosomes coiled around histone proteins
RNA in place of DNA, packed inside a protein capsid
w: Bacteria usually carry one circular chromosome in the nucleoid region, often with small extra circles of DNA called plasmids.

n.1: Multiple linear chromosomes in a nucleus describe the human (eukaryotic) cell, not the bacterium.
n.2: Histone packaging into chromatin is a eukaryotic feature.
n.3: Some viruses carry RNA inside a capsid. Bacteria are cells and store their genes in DNA.

q: A neuron and a white blood cell from the same patient differ greatly in shape and function. Which statement best explains this difference?
o: Each cell type expresses a different set of genes.
Each cell type lost the genes that it does not use.
Each cell type arose from a different mutation.
Each cell type holds a different set of genes.
w: All body cells descend from one zygote by mitosis and carry the same DNA. Cells differentiate by switching different genes on and off (gene regulation), so each type makes its own set of proteins.

n.1: Differentiated cells keep the full set of genes; genes they do not need are switched off, not deleted.
n.2: Differentiation is controlled gene expression, not mutation; mutations are rare copying errors.
n.3: Body cells of one person carry the same DNA; what differs is which genes are used.

q: A patient receives a bone marrow transplant so that the marrow can again produce red cells, white cells and platelets. Which donated cells make this possible?
o: Mature white blood cells that change their type
Embryonic stem cells that can form any cell
Mature red blood cells that divide by mitosis
Adult stem cells that form several blood cells
w: Bone marrow holds adult (blood-forming) stem cells: unspecialized cells that divide and differentiate into red cells, white cells and platelets. Adult stem cells form a more limited range of cell types than embryonic stem cells.

n.0: Mature white blood cells are already specialized; they do not convert into red cells or platelets.
n.1: Embryonic stem cells come from an early embryo, not from an adult donor's bone marrow.
n.2: Mature red blood cells have no nucleus and cannot divide.

q: Cells of the pancreas secrete large amounts of protein-based digestive enzymes into the small intestine. Which organelle would be especially extensive in these cells?
o: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum
Peroxisomes
Rough endoplasmic reticulum
Lysosomes
w: Rough ER is studded with ribosomes and makes and folds proteins destined for secretion, so cells that export a lot of protein have extensive rough ER.

n.0: Smooth ER has no ribosomes. It makes lipids and steroids and detoxifies drugs, so it suits steroid-secreting or liver cells.
n.1: Peroxisomes break down fatty acids and toxins and convert hydrogen peroxide; they do not produce secreted proteins.
n.3: Lysosomes digest worn-out organelles and engulfed material inside the cell; they do not make secreted proteins.

q: Liver cells of a patient who takes a daily anticonvulsant drug show a marked increase in an organelle that detoxifies drugs and makes lipids. Which organelle is it?
o: Golgi apparatus
Smooth endoplasmic reticulum
Rough endoplasmic reticulum
Nucleolus
w: Smooth ER lacks ribosomes and carries out lipid and steroid synthesis and detoxification, which is why it is prominent in liver cells exposed to drugs.

n.0: The Golgi modifies, sorts and packages proteins and lipids; it does not detoxify drugs.
n.2: Rough ER makes proteins on its ribosomes; detoxification and lipid synthesis are smooth ER jobs.
n.3: The nucleolus makes ribosomal RNA and assembles ribosome subunits inside the nucleus.

q: A researcher damages a dense region inside the nucleus of a cultured cell, and the cell soon stops assembling new ribosomes. Which structure was most likely damaged?
o: The centrosome
The nucleolus
The nuclear envelope
The Golgi apparatus
w: The nucleolus is the dense region inside the nucleus that makes ribosomal RNA and assembles ribosome subunits.

n.0: The centrosome sits in the cytoplasm and organizes microtubules and the spindle.
n.2: The nuclear envelope is the double membrane around the nucleus, not a dense region inside it, and it does not build ribosomes.
n.3: The Golgi is in the cytoplasm and packages proteins; it does not make ribosomal RNA.

q: On a quiz, a student writes that the Golgi apparatus makes proteins. Which correction describes the role of the Golgi accurately?
o: It breaks down proteins with hydrolytic enzymes.
It synthesizes lipids and steroid hormones.
It modifies and packages proteins made elsewhere.
It copies DNA into messenger RNA for export.
w: Proteins are made by ribosomes (many on rough ER). The Golgi then modifies, sorts and packages them into vesicles, like a post office.

n.0: Breaking down material with hydrolytic enzymes is the job of lysosomes.
n.1: Lipid and steroid synthesis happens in the smooth ER.
n.3: Copying DNA into mRNA is transcription, which takes place in the nucleus.

q: Heart muscle cells contract continuously throughout life and need a steady supply of ATP. Compared with less active cells, which organelle would these cells contain in especially large numbers?
o: Mitochondria
Lysosomes
Peroxisomes
Ribosomes
w: Mitochondria carry out aerobic cellular respiration and make most of a cell's ATP, so highly active cells such as cardiac and skeletal muscle cells contain many of them.

n.1: Lysosomes digest worn-out parts and engulfed particles; they do not supply ATP.
n.2: Peroxisomes break down fatty acids and hydrogen peroxide but are not the main ATP producers.
n.3: Ribosomes make proteins. ATP production is the job of mitochondria.

q: A neutrophil engulfs a bacterium, enclosing it in a vesicle. Which organelle then fuses with the vesicle and digests the bacterium using hydrolytic enzymes in an acidic interior?
o: Golgi apparatus
Smooth endoplasmic reticulum
Peroxisome
Lysosome
w: Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes in an acidic interior and digest engulfed bacteria, food particles and worn-out organelles.

n.0: The Golgi packages proteins and makes lysosomes, but it does not itself digest engulfed bacteria.
n.1: Smooth ER makes lipids and detoxifies drugs; it does not digest engulfed microbes.
n.2: Peroxisomes break down fatty acids and toxins and convert hydrogen peroxide with catalase; they are not the acidic digestive sacs.

q: Cells lining the trachea move a layer of mucus and trapped particles up toward the throat. Which structures on the surface of these cells produce this movement?
o: A single long flagellum on each cell
Many short cilia on each cell
Centrioles anchored at the cell surface
Many microvilli on each cell
w: Cilia are many short, hairlike projections that beat together, as in the airway. Flagella are one or a few long whips, as on sperm.

n.0: Flagella are long and usually single, and they propel a cell such as a sperm rather than sweeping material across a surface.
n.2: Centrioles organize microtubules and the spindle; they do not themselves beat to move mucus.
n.3: Microvilli are nonmotile folds that increase surface area for absorption; they do not beat to move mucus.

q: A cancer drug blocks the assembly of microtubules from tubulin. Which cell process would this drug most directly interfere with?
o: Synthesis of steroids in the smooth ER
Formation of the mitotic spindle
Production of ATP on the cristae
Synthesis of ribosomal RNA
w: Microtubules form the spindle fibers that move chromosomes during cell division, so blocking them stops dividing cells, which is why such drugs are used against cancer.

n.0: Steroid synthesis is carried out by smooth ER enzymes, not by the cytoskeleton.
n.2: ATP is made by the electron transport chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane, not by microtubules.
n.3: Ribosomal RNA is made in the nucleolus and does not depend on microtubule assembly.

q: Which observation provides the strongest support for the hypothesis that mitochondria descended from prokaryotes engulfed by an ancestral cell?
o: They have their own circular DNA and a double membrane.
They produce most of the ATP made by the cell.
They are found in plant cells as well as animal cells.
They are more numerous in muscle cells than in skin cells.
w: Endosymbiotic theory is supported by features mitochondria share with bacteria: their own circular DNA and ribosomes, a double membrane, and division by binary fission.

n.1: Producing most of the ATP is the function of mitochondria, not evidence of where they came from.
n.2: Being present in plants and animals is true, but it says nothing about a prokaryotic origin.
n.3: Higher numbers in active cells reflect energy demand, not ancestry.

q: The inner membrane of a mitochondrion is folded into many cristae. What is the main advantage of this folding for the cell?
o: It anchors ribosomes that make secreted proteins.
It gives the electron transport chain more area.
It holds chlorophyll for capturing light energy.
It stores calcium ions for muscle contraction.
w: The electron transport chain sits in the inner membrane (cristae) and makes most of the cell's ATP, so more folds mean more membrane for ATP production.

n.0: Ribosomes making secreted proteins are attached to the rough ER.
n.2: Chlorophyll is held in the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts, not mitochondria.
n.3: Calcium storage for contraction is the job of the sarcoplasmic reticulum, a smooth ER in muscle.

q: Oxygen moves from the alveoli, where its concentration is high, into lung capillary cells by passing directly through the phospholipid bilayer. Which transport process does this describe?
o: Facilitated diffusion through channels
Active transport by membrane pumps
Simple diffusion
Osmosis through aquaporins
w: Small nonpolar molecules such as O₂ and CO₂ cross the bilayer directly, from high to low concentration, with no protein and no ATP: simple diffusion.

n.0: Facilitated diffusion needs a channel or carrier protein. Oxygen is small and nonpolar, so it passes through the lipid bilayer itself.
n.1: Active transport uses ATP to move substances against a gradient. Oxygen is moving down its gradient.
n.3: Osmosis is the movement of water, not of a dissolved gas such as oxygen.

q: Glucose enters a muscle cell through GLUT carrier proteins, moving from higher concentration in the blood to lower concentration in the cell without using ATP. Which process is this?
o: Facilitated diffusion
Active transport by a pump
Simple diffusion across the bilayer
Pinocytosis by vesicles
w: Movement down a concentration gradient through a carrier or channel protein, without ATP, is facilitated diffusion.

n.1: Active transport uses ATP and moves substances from low to high concentration. A carrier protein alone does not make transport active.
n.2: Simple diffusion passes straight through the bilayer with no protein. Glucose is too large and polar to do that.
n.3: Pinocytosis takes in droplets of fluid by vesicle and uses ATP; it is not carrier-mediated transport of single molecules.

q: In a lab, red blood cells are placed in a 5% sodium chloride solution, which is hypertonic to the cells. What will most likely happen to the cells?
o: There is no net water movement, so the cells keep their shape.
Water enters the cells, which swell and undergo hemolysis.
Sodium enters the cells, which swell as solute builds up.
Water leaves the cells, which shrink and undergo crenation.
w: A hypertonic solution has more solute outside the cell, so water leaves by osmosis and the red blood cells shrink (crenation).

n.0: No net water movement describes an isotonic solution such as 0.9% NaCl, not a 5% solution.
n.1: Swelling and hemolysis happen in a hypotonic solution, where water moves into the cell.
n.2: Osmosis is the movement of water, not solute. The cells lose water and shrink.

q: A selectively permeable membrane separates a 2% sucrose solution on side A from a 10% sucrose solution on side B. Sucrose cannot cross the membrane. What net movement will occur?
o: Sucrose moves from side B to side A.
Neither water nor sucrose will move.
Water moves from side A to side B.
Water moves from side B to side A.
w: Step 1: side B has the higher solute concentration, so it has the lower water concentration. Step 2: in osmosis water moves toward the higher solute concentration, so the net flow is from A to B.

n.0: The stem states sucrose cannot cross, and osmosis moves water rather than solute.
n.1: Water can still cross the membrane. The sucrose difference drives osmosis even though sucrose itself cannot move.
n.3: Water moves toward the side with more solute (B), not away from it.

q: A nursing student is reviewing the sodium-potassium pump in the plasma membrane of a resting neuron. Which statement about the pump is accurate?
o: It uses ATP to move both ions against their gradients.
It moves 2 Na⁺ out and 3 K⁺ in during each cycle.
It is facilitated diffusion, since it uses a carrier protein.
It moves both ions down their concentration gradients.
w: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump is active transport: it spends ATP to push Na⁺ out and K⁺ in, each from low to high concentration.

n.1: The numbers are reversed: the pump moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in.
n.2: Using a carrier protein does not make transport passive. The pump uses ATP, which facilitated diffusion does not.
n.3: Movement down a gradient needs no ATP. The pump works against both gradients.

q: A wilted lettuce leaf is soaked in pure tap water and becomes crisp again within an hour. Which explanation best accounts for this change?
o: Water enters the cells, which then swell until they lyse and collapse.
Solutes enter the cells by active transport, so the cells shrink.
Water leaves the cells, and plasmolysis pulls the membranes inward.
Water enters the cells, and the walls let them become turgid.
w: Pure water is hypotonic to the leaf cells, so water enters by osmosis. The cellulose wall resists the swelling, and the cells become turgid (firm) instead of bursting.

n.0: Animal cells such as red blood cells lyse in hypotonic solutions. Plant cells are protected by the cell wall.
n.1: Solute gain would draw water in, not make the cells shrink, and pure water has almost no solute to take up.
n.2: Plasmolysis happens in a hypertonic solution, when water leaves the cell. That would make the leaf wilt more.

q: A patient receives intravenous fluid of 0.9% sodium chloride rather than sterile pure water. Which statement best explains this choice at the level of the red blood cells?
o: It is hypotonic, so water moves into dehydrated red cells.
It is isotonic, so red cells neither gain nor lose water overall.
It supplies the sodium that red cells absorb by active transport.
It is hypertonic, so excess water is drawn out of the red cells.
w: Normal saline (0.9% NaCl) is isotonic to human cells, so there is no net water movement and the red cells keep their shape. Pure water is hypotonic and would cause hemolysis.

n.0: 0.9% NaCl is isotonic, not hypotonic. Pure water is the hypotonic fluid that would make red cells swell and burst.
n.2: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump moves sodium out of cells, not in, and the choice of saline is about tonicity.
n.3: 0.9% NaCl is not hypertonic. A hypertonic fluid would make red cells shrink (crenation).

q: LDL particles carrying cholesterol bind to specific proteins on the surface of a liver cell, and the membrane then folds inward to bring them in. Which process is this?
o: Phagocytosis of a large particle
Exocytosis by a secretory vesicle
Receptor-mediated endocytosis
Facilitated diffusion via a carrier
w: Binding of a specific substance to surface receptors followed by inward folding of the membrane into a vesicle is receptor-mediated endocytosis, the route for cholesterol (LDL).

n.0: Phagocytosis is endocytosis of large particles such as bacteria by cells such as neutrophils, not receptor-specific uptake of LDL.
n.1: Exocytosis releases material from the cell; this material is entering.
n.3: Facilitated diffusion moves single molecules through channels or carriers, without forming vesicles.

q: A nursing student is matching membrane processes to examples for a study sheet. Which pairing is correct?
o: Facilitated diffusion: the pump that moves Na⁺ and K⁺ ions
Active transport: oxygen moving into a red blood cell
Exocytosis: a neuron releasing neurotransmitter from vesicles
Phagocytosis: a cell taking in droplets of extracellular fluid
w: Exocytosis releases material from the cell when a vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane, as in neurotransmitter, hormone and enzyme secretion.

n.0: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump uses ATP to move ions against their gradients, which is active transport.
n.1: Oxygen enters red blood cells by simple diffusion down its gradient, with no ATP.
n.3: Taking in fluid droplets is pinocytosis (cell drinking). Phagocytosis engulfs solid particles such as bacteria.

q: A student sets up a model in which a dye diffuses across a membrane from a concentrated solution into a dilute one. Which change would increase the rate of diffusion?
o: Using a dye that has much larger molecules
Making the membrane twice as thick as before
Diluting the more concentrated solution
Raising the temperature of the solutions
w: Diffusion is faster at higher temperature, with a steeper concentration gradient, smaller molecules, greater surface area and a shorter distance.

n.0: Larger molecules diffuse more slowly than smaller ones.
n.1: A thicker membrane increases the distance, which slows diffusion.
n.2: Diluting the concentrated side makes the gradient less steep, which slows diffusion.

q: A textbook diagram labels the plasma membrane of an animal cell as a fluid mosaic. Which description of the membrane is consistent with this model?
o: A rigid layer of cellulose that small solutes pass through
A phospholipid bilayer that ions cross with no protein help
A double layer of proteins coated with phospholipid heads
A phospholipid bilayer with proteins that drift within it
w: The fluid mosaic model describes a phospholipid bilayer in which proteins, cholesterol (in animal cells) and glycoproteins are embedded and can move laterally, forming a selectively permeable barrier.

n.0: A cellulose layer describes a plant cell wall, which lies outside the plasma membrane.
n.1: Ions are charged and cannot easily cross the hydrophobic interior; they need channel or carrier proteins.
n.2: The membrane's framework is a phospholipid bilayer, with proteins embedded in it, not a protein double layer.

q: Leaf cells of the pond plant Elodea are placed in concentrated salt water and viewed under a microscope. Which change is seen in the cells?
o: Water leaves, and the membrane pulls away from the wall.
Salt enters, and the swollen cells burst their walls.
Water leaves, and the cell walls shrivel and crenate.
Water enters, and the cells press firmly on their walls.
w: Concentrated salt water is hypertonic to the cells, so water leaves by osmosis. The rigid cellulose wall keeps its shape while the membrane shrinks away from it: plasmolysis.

n.1: Osmosis moves water, not salt, and here the cells lose water; the wall also keeps plant cells from bursting.
n.2: Crenation is the shrinking of wall-less red blood cells. A plant cell wall is rigid and keeps its shape; the membrane pulls away from it instead.
n.3: Water entry and turgor follow a hypotonic solution such as pure water; concentrated salt water is hypertonic.

q: A researcher finds that the DNA content of a dividing skin cell doubles before any chromosomes become visible. During which phase did this doubling occur?
o: The S phase of interphase
The G2 phase of interphase
The G1 phase of interphase
Prophase of mitosis
w: DNA is replicated during the S (synthesis) phase of interphase, turning each chromosome into two sister chromatids before mitosis begins.

n.1: G2 follows S phase. The DNA is already doubled, and the cell is preparing to divide.
n.2: G1 is a growth phase before DNA synthesis begins.
n.3: In prophase the already-replicated chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes; replication happened earlier, in S phase.

q: An onion root tip slide shows a cell in which identical sets of condensed chromosomes are being pulled toward opposite ends. Which phase of mitosis is shown?
o: Prophase
Anaphase
Telophase
Metaphase
w: In anaphase, sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles, so two identical sets of chromosomes are seen moving apart.

n.0: In prophase chromosomes condense and the spindle forms; chromatids have not yet separated.
n.2: In telophase the chromosomes have reached the poles, nuclear envelopes re-form and chromosomes decondense.
n.3: In metaphase the chromosomes are lined up at the cell's equator, not moving toward the poles.

q: A human skin cell with 46 chromosomes completes mitosis and cytokinesis. Which result is expected?
o: Two identical cells, each with 46 chromosomes
Four haploid cells, each with 23 chromosomes
Four diploid cells, each genetically different
Two haploid cells, each with 23 chromosomes
w: Mitosis produces 2 genetically identical diploid daughter cells: 46 chromosomes in, 46 in each daughter cell.

n.1: Four haploid cells is the result of meiosis, which makes gametes, not of mitosis in a skin cell.
n.2: Mitosis makes two cells, not four, and they are genetically identical to the parent.
n.3: Mitosis keeps the chromosome number the same; it does not halve it.

q: During anaphase I of meiosis in a human testis, which structures separate and move to opposite poles of the cell?
o: Single chromatids drawn from all four strands of each tetrad
Haploid daughter cells pinched apart at a cleavage furrow
Homologous chromosomes, each still made of two chromatids
Sister chromatids, each becoming its own chromosome
w: Anaphase I separates homologous chromosomes; each still consists of two sister chromatids joined at the centromere. Sister chromatids separate later, in anaphase II.

n.0: The four chromatids of a tetrad do not split up individually in anaphase I; whole homologs, each with two chromatids, move apart.
n.1: Pinching apart the cytoplasm is cytokinesis, which follows telophase; it is not what moves to the poles in anaphase I.
n.3: Sister chromatids separate in anaphase II of meiosis and in mitotic anaphase, not in anaphase I.

q: Two sisters with the same parents differ genetically partly because segments were exchanged between homologous chromosomes while their parents' gametes formed. When does this exchange take place?
o: Metaphase of mitosis
Prophase II of meiosis
Anaphase I of meiosis
Prophase I of meiosis
w: Crossing over happens in prophase I, when homologous chromosomes pair up (synapsis) as tetrads and exchange segments.

n.0: Homologous chromosomes do not pair in mitosis, so there is no crossing over.
n.1: Homologs are no longer paired in prophase II, so crossing over between them does not occur then.
n.2: Anaphase I is when homologs separate; the exchange had already happened in prophase I.

q: During meiosis I, both copies of chromosome 21 end up in one egg, which a normal sperm then fertilizes. What will the zygote most likely have?
o: 45 chromosomes, the pattern seen in Turner syndrome
47 chromosomes, with an XXY set of sex chromosomes
45 chromosomes, with one copy of chromosome 21
47 chromosomes, including three copies of chromosome 21
w: Step 1: nondisjunction gives the egg 24 chromosomes, including two copies of chromosome 21. Step 2: adding a normal sperm's 23 gives 47, with three copies of chromosome 21 (trisomy 21, Down syndrome).

n.0: Turner syndrome (45,X) is a missing sex chromosome. This egg has an extra chromosome, so the total rises above 46.
n.1: XXY (Klinefelter syndrome) involves the sex chromosomes, but the nondisjunction here involved chromosome 21.
n.2: A zygote with one chromosome 21 would come from an egg that received no copy. Here the egg received both copies.

q: A student compares mitosis and meiosis in a table. Which event occurs in meiosis but does not occur in mitosis?
o: Replication of DNA before division
Pairing of homologous chromosomes
Separation of sister chromatids
Formation of a spindle from microtubules
w: Homologous chromosomes pair (synapsis) and form tetrads only in prophase I of meiosis. The other events happen in both processes.

n.0: DNA is replicated once, during S phase, before both mitosis and meiosis.
n.2: Sister chromatids separate in mitotic anaphase and in anaphase II of meiosis.
n.3: A microtubule spindle moves chromosomes in both mitosis and meiosis.

q: A karyotype is prepared from a body cell of a healthy human female. Which description of her chromosomes is accurate?
o: 22 pairs of autosomes plus one pair of X chromosomes
23 pairs of autosomes plus one pair of X chromosomes
22 pairs of autosomes plus one X and one Y chromosome
46 pairs of chromosomes, including two X chromosomes
w: Human body cells have 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs: 22 pairs of autosomes and 1 pair of sex chromosomes, XX in a female.

n.1: This adds up to 24 pairs (48 chromosomes). There are 22 pairs of autosomes, not 23.
n.2: An X and a Y is the male sex chromosome pair.
n.3: Humans have 46 chromosomes, which is 23 pairs, not 46 pairs.

q: At the end of mitosis, a plant root cell divides its cytoplasm differently from an animal cell. Which structure forms between the two new plant cells?
o: A nuclear envelope that splits the cell
A centriole pair that pulls the cell apart
A cleavage furrow that pinches inward
A cell plate that becomes a new wall
w: In plant cells, cytokinesis builds a cell plate across the middle that develops into a new cell wall. Animal cells pinch in with a cleavage furrow.

n.0: Nuclear envelopes re-form around each set of chromosomes in telophase; they do not divide the cytoplasm.
n.1: Most plant cells lack centrioles, and centrioles organize the spindle rather than splitting the cytoplasm.
n.2: A cleavage furrow is how animal cells divide their cytoplasm; the rigid plant wall prevents pinching.

q: Cells in a tumor keep dividing even when they are crowded and their DNA is damaged. Which part of cell cycle control has most likely failed?
o: Checkpoints that halt the cycle
Crossing over in prophase I
DNA replication during S phase
Cytokinesis after telophase
w: Checkpoints normally stop the cycle when DNA is damaged or conditions are wrong. When they fail, cells divide uncontrollably, which leads to cancer.

n.1: Crossing over occurs in meiosis, not in the mitotic divisions of tumor cells.
n.2: S phase copies DNA; uncontrolled division comes from failed control, not from replication itself.
n.3: Cytokinesis is the final split of the cytoplasm; it does not decide whether a cell divides.

q: Under a microscope, a dividing cell shows condensing chromosomes, a forming spindle and a breaking-down nuclear envelope. Which phase is shown?
o: Metaphase
Prophase
Interphase
Telophase
w: In prophase the chromosomes condense, the spindle forms and the nuclear envelope breaks down.

n.0: In metaphase the chromosomes are already lined up at the cell equator.
n.2: In interphase the chromosomes are not condensed and no spindle is present.
n.3: In telophase nuclear envelopes re-form and chromosomes decondense, the reverse of this.

q: A human cell entering meiosis II has 23 chromosomes, each made of two sister chromatids. What happens during anaphase II?
o: The DNA replicates again.
Sister chromatids separate.
Homologs pair and cross over.
Homologous chromosomes separate.
w: Meiosis II works like mitosis: in anaphase II the sister chromatids separate to opposite poles, giving haploid cells with single chromatids.

n.0: DNA replicates once, before meiosis I; there is no replication between the two divisions.
n.2: Pairing and crossing over happen in prophase I.
n.3: Homologous chromosomes separated earlier, in anaphase I.

q: During a sprint, a runner's leg muscle cells run short of oxygen. Which stage of glucose breakdown can continue to supply these cells with ATP?
o: The Krebs cycle in the matrix
Glycolysis in the cytoplasm
Pyruvate oxidation in the matrix
The electron transport chain
w: Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm and needs no oxygen, netting 2 ATP per glucose. With lactic acid fermentation regenerating what glycolysis needs, it keeps running when oxygen is short.

n.0: The Krebs cycle depends on the electron transport chain, which needs oxygen, so it slows when oxygen runs short.
n.2: Pyruvate oxidation makes no ATP and stalls without oxygen, since the electron transport chain no longer regenerates NAD+.
n.3: The electron transport chain requires oxygen as the final electron acceptor, so it stops without oxygen.

q: A student writes that the Krebs cycle produces most of the ATP in aerobic cellular respiration. Which stage actually produces the most ATP per molecule of glucose?
o: Pyruvate oxidation in the matrix
Lactic acid fermentation
Glycolysis in the cytoplasm
The electron transport chain
w: The electron transport chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane (cristae) uses NADH and FADH2 from earlier stages to make most of the ATP from each glucose.

n.0: Pyruvate oxidation releases CO₂ and makes NADH but produces little ATP directly.
n.1: Fermentation is anaerobic and yields only the 2 ATP from glycolysis.
n.2: Glycolysis nets 2 ATP per glucose, a small share of the total.

q: A patient breathes in oxygen that eventually reaches the mitochondria of her cells. What is the role of this oxygen in aerobic cellular respiration?
o: It accepts electrons from the chain and forms water.
It converts pyruvate into acetyl-CoA.
It splits glucose into two molecules of pyruvate.
It combines with carbon to form carbon dioxide.
w: Oxygen is the final electron acceptor of the electron transport chain; it picks up electrons and hydrogen ions to form water.

n.1: Pyruvate is oxidized to acetyl-CoA by NAD+ in the matrix, releasing CO2; oxygen is not used in this step.
n.2: Glycolysis splits glucose into pyruvate without using any oxygen.
n.3: The CO₂ exhaled comes from carbon in glucose released during pyruvate oxidation and the Krebs cycle, not from the oxygen breathed in.

q: Bread dough rises when yeast cells, deprived of oxygen inside the dough, break down sugar and release a gas. Which process is responsible, and what does it produce?
o: Aerobic respiration, producing water and oxygen gas
Lactic acid fermentation, producing lactic acid and CO₂
Photosynthesis, producing glucose and oxygen gas
Alcoholic fermentation, producing ethanol and CO₂
w: Without oxygen, yeast carry out alcoholic fermentation: glycolysis followed by conversion of pyruvate to ethanol and carbon dioxide. The CO₂ bubbles make the dough rise.

n.0: The yeast lack oxygen, and aerobic respiration consumes oxygen rather than producing it.
n.1: Lactic acid fermentation occurs in human muscle and releases no CO₂, so it would not raise dough.
n.2: Yeast are fungi and cannot photosynthesize; photosynthesis also uses CO₂ rather than releasing it.

q: A toxin blocks the electron transport chain in a patient's cells. Which change in those cells would be expected?
o: Glucose is broken down directly into CO₂ in the cytoplasm.
Oxygen use rises, as more is needed to accept electrons.
ATP output holds steady, as the Krebs cycle makes up the loss.
ATP output drops, and cells shift to lactic acid fermentation.
w: Step 1: the electron transport chain makes most of the cell's ATP, so blocking it causes a sharp fall in ATP. Step 2: cells fall back on glycolysis, which needs no oxygen, regenerating its needs by lactic acid fermentation.

n.0: CO₂ is released in the mitochondria (pyruvate oxidation and Krebs cycle), not from glucose in the cytoplasm.
n.1: Oxygen is used only as the final electron acceptor of the chain, so a blocked chain uses less oxygen, not more.
n.2: The Krebs cycle makes only a little ATP and stalls when the chain stops regenerating NAD+ and FAD, so it cannot replace the chain's output.

q: A researcher isolates the fluid-filled interior (matrix) of mitochondria. Which stage of cellular respiration would be active in this fraction?
o: The electron transport chain
The Krebs cycle
The Calvin cycle
Glycolysis
w: The Krebs (citric acid) cycle runs in the mitochondrial matrix, releasing CO2 and loading NADH and FADH2.

n.0: The electron transport chain is built into the inner membrane (cristae), not the matrix fluid.
n.2: The Calvin cycle is part of photosynthesis in the chloroplast stroma.
n.3: Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm, outside the mitochondria.

q: Which stages of aerobic respiration release the carbon dioxide that a person exhales?
o: Pyruvate oxidation and the Krebs cycle
Lactic acid fermentation in the cytoplasm
Glycolysis, as glucose splits into pyruvate
The electron transport chain, using oxygen
w: CO2 is released when pyruvate is oxidized to acetyl-CoA and during the Krebs cycle, both in the mitochondrial matrix.

n.1: Lactic acid fermentation releases no CO2.
n.2: Glycolysis splits glucose into pyruvate without releasing CO2.
n.3: The chain uses oxygen to form water; it releases no CO2.

q: Glycolysis breaks down one molecule of glucose. Which net products does it form?
o: 2 pyruvate, 4 ATP and 2 NADH
2 acetyl-CoA, 2 ATP and 2 CO2
6 CO2, 6 H2O and 2 ATP
2 pyruvate, 2 ATP and 2 NADH
w: Glycolysis splits glucose into 2 pyruvate, with a net gain of 2 ATP (4 made, 2 spent) and 2 NADH.

n.0: 4 ATP is the gross yield; 2 ATP are spent at the start, so the net is 2.
n.1: Acetyl-CoA and CO2 come from pyruvate oxidation in the mitochondria, after glycolysis.
n.2: 6 CO2 and 6 H2O are the products of complete aerobic respiration, not glycolysis.

q: A cell completely breaks down 3 molecules of glucose by aerobic respiration. How many molecules of carbon dioxide are released?
w: C6H12O6 + 6 O2 -> 6 CO2 + 6 H2O, so each glucose releases 6 CO2: 3 x 6 = 18.

n.0: 12 CO2 corresponds to two glucose molecules, not three.
n.1: 6 CO2 is the amount for one glucose; the cell broke down three.
n.3: Each glucose has six carbons, so it releases six CO2, not one.

q: During lactic acid fermentation in muscle, what does converting pyruvate to lactic acid accomplish for the cell?
o: It supplies oxygen to the electron transport chain.
It releases CO2 that feeds the Krebs cycle.
It makes most of the ATP the cell uses.
It regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can go on.
w: Glycolysis needs NAD+. Without oxygen, turning pyruvate into lactic acid regenerates NAD+, so glycolysis keeps making its 2 ATP per glucose.

n.0: Fermentation makes no oxygen; it is how cells cope when oxygen is lacking.
n.1: Lactic acid fermentation releases no CO2, and the Krebs cycle stalls without oxygen.
n.2: Fermentation adds no ATP beyond the 2 from glycolysis; most ATP comes from the chain.

q: A student says cellular respiration is the same as breathing. Which statement best corrects the student?
o: Breathing exchanges gases; cellular respiration makes ATP in cells.
Breathing makes ATP; cellular respiration exchanges gases in lungs.
Cellular respiration makes O2 that breathing then removes.
Both terms describe gas exchange in the alveoli of the lungs.
w: Breathing moves air in and out of the lungs. Cellular respiration is the chemical breakdown of glucose inside cells to make ATP, using O2 and producing CO2.

n.1: The roles are reversed: cells make ATP, and the lungs exchange gases.
n.2: Cellular respiration uses O2 and produces CO2; it does not make oxygen.
n.3: Cellular respiration takes place in the cells' cytoplasm and mitochondria, not in the alveoli.

q: At night, a houseplant takes in oxygen and gives off carbon dioxide. Which process explains this exchange?
o: Cellular respiration in mitochondria
Fermentation in the central vacuole
Photosynthesis in the chloroplasts
The Calvin cycle in the chloroplast stroma
w: Plants carry out cellular respiration in their mitochondria all the time, using O2 and releasing CO2. Without light, photosynthesis stops, so respiration's gas exchange shows.

n.1: Fermentation is anaerobic and uses no oxygen; the vacuole stores water and wastes.
n.2: Photosynthesis uses CO2 and releases O2, the reverse, and needs light.
n.3: The Calvin cycle fixes CO2 into sugar rather than releasing it.

q: In a leaf cell, water molecules are split and oxygen gas is released during photosynthesis. Where in the chloroplast does this happen?
o: In the inner membrane, during electron transport
In the thylakoids, during the light reactions
In the cytoplasm, during glycolysis
In the stroma, during the Calvin cycle
w: The light-dependent reactions take place in the thylakoid membranes. There water is split, O₂ is released, and ATP and NADPH are made for the Calvin cycle.

n.0: Electron transport on an inner membrane that ends with O₂ forming water describes mitochondria, the reverse of releasing O₂.
n.2: Glycolysis in the cytoplasm is part of respiration and neither splits water nor releases oxygen.
n.3: The Calvin cycle in the stroma fixes CO₂ into sugar; it does not split water.

q: A plant biology quiz asks about the light-independent reactions (Calvin cycle) of photosynthesis. Which statement about the Calvin cycle is accurate?
o: It requires darkness and stops once light is present.
It releases CO₂ in the matrix of the mitochondria.
It splits water and releases oxygen in the thylakoids.
It fixes CO₂ into sugar using ATP and NADPH.
w: The Calvin cycle takes place in the stroma and uses the ATP and NADPH from the light reactions to fix carbon dioxide into sugar.

n.0: Light-independent means it does not use light directly. It runs in daylight, powered by ATP and NADPH from the light reactions.
n.1: Releasing CO₂ in the mitochondrial matrix describes the Krebs cycle of respiration.
n.2: Splitting water and releasing O₂ happen in the light-dependent reactions in the thylakoids.

q: A teacher asks the class to compare cellular respiration with photosynthesis in a green plant. Which statement is accurate?
o: Respiration happens in chloroplasts and photosynthesis in mitochondria.
Respiration releases CO₂ and photosynthesis releases O₂.
Respiration releases O₂ and photosynthesis releases CO₂.
Plants carry out photosynthesis instead of cellular respiration.
w: Respiration: glucose + O₂ -> CO₂ + H₂O + ATP. Photosynthesis: CO₂ + H₂O + light -> glucose + O₂. The equations are roughly reversed, and plants do both.

n.0: The organelles are reversed: respiration uses mitochondria and photosynthesis uses chloroplasts.
n.2: The gases are reversed: respiration uses O₂ and releases CO₂, and photosynthesis does the opposite.
n.3: Plants have mitochondria and carry out cellular respiration as well as photosynthesis.

q: Most leaves look green in sunlight. Which statement best explains this in terms of how chlorophyll interacts with light?
o: It absorbs mostly red and blue light and reflects green.
It absorbs mostly green light and reflects red and blue.
It absorbs mostly green light and turns it into glucose.
It absorbs ultraviolet light and gives it off as green.
w: Chlorophyll absorbs mainly red and blue wavelengths for photosynthesis and reflects green, which is the color we see.

n.1: This is reversed. A pigment looks the color it reflects, so green is the color chlorophyll absorbs least.
n.2: Green light is mostly reflected, so it contributes little energy to making glucose.
n.3: Leaves are green because of reflected green light, not because chlorophyll converts ultraviolet light into green.

q: Which molecules made by the light-dependent reactions supply the energy for the Calvin cycle?
o: ATP and NADPH
NADH and FADH2
Carbon dioxide and water
Oxygen and glucose
w: The light reactions in the thylakoids make ATP and NADPH; the Calvin cycle in the stroma spends them to fix CO2 into sugar.

n.1: NADH and FADH2 are electron carriers of cellular respiration.
n.2: CO2 and water are raw materials of photosynthesis, not energy carriers.
n.3: O2 is a by-product released to the air, and glucose is a product of the Calvin cycle.

q: Through which leaf structures does carbon dioxide enter for photosynthesis?
o: Root hairs in the soil
Thylakoids inside chloroplasts
Stomata on the leaf surface
Xylem vessels in the veins
w: CO2 diffuses into the leaf, and O2 out, through stomata: pores controlled by guard cells.

n.0: Root hairs absorb water and minerals from the soil.
n.1: Thylakoids host the light reactions inside the chloroplast; they are not openings to the air.
n.3: Xylem carries water up from the roots, not CO2 from the air.

q: A plant is given water containing a heavy isotope of oxygen. During photosynthesis, where will most of the heavy oxygen end up?
o: In the glucose the leaf produces
In the carbon dioxide it absorbs
In the chlorophyll of the thylakoids
In the oxygen gas the leaf releases
w: Water is split in the light reactions, and its oxygen atoms are released as O2. The O2 from photosynthesis comes from water, not from CO2.

n.0: The oxygen in glucose comes from CO2 fixed in the Calvin cycle.
n.1: CO2 is taken in from the air; the labeled water does not become CO2.
